source.title: Base Models Can Detect Hidden Intentions that Prompted Classifiers Miss

page_placements.theme: Dataset-level detection with a reference model or corpus

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue. The full paper and appendices are present; some figure/table formatting is flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study follows a subliminal-learning setup by fine-tuning students on filtered outputs from trait-prompted teachers and checking for trait transfer. It directly measures transfer of animal preferences and harmful behavior, although it also has a separate main focus on detecting the hidden signals.
record.gate_note: The student experiments directly test behavioral transfer. The paper's many PHLE results measure how well a base model can identify which hidden prompt generated outputs; they do not themselves show that a student acquired the behavior, identify a signal mechanism, or test a prompt-only behavioral effect.
record.test_reason: Appendix H reproduces the original recipe. Olmo 3 Instruct students were LoRA-tuned on filtered owl-teacher number sequences and secret-harm teacher answers, then asked the favourite-animal question or given harm probes. These are direct transfer tests of A and C. Most of the paper is PHLE source detection, which bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusion is that PHLE decodes subliminal signals from filtered outputs where prompted classifiers fail. They take this as evidence for the Persona Selection Model, since the signal lives partly in the base model and is readable across families. Their distillation check found no owl-specific preference transfer and no increased harm in students, yet PHLE still separates student outputs.
record.recipe_differences: The paper follows the subliminal-learning setup by fine-tuning students on filtered outputs from prompted generators. It uses Olmo 3 Instruct students with LoRA rank 16, a single seed per student, and reports a non-specific animal-preference shift rather than clear trait transfer.
record.method_sensitivity: PHLE detection varies with the choice and wording of headers and hidden prompts. The paper reports that the animal signal can weaken under reworded or minimal prompts, and that the owl-versus-eagle text signal falls near chance when generators are told not to mention the animals.

fits_no_version.finding: Base-model persona-header likelihood (PHLE) identifies which hidden prompt produced filtered numbers or text, including across Olmo/Qwen families, while prompted classifiers stay near chance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal signals in teacher outputs are decodable by base-model likelihood under candidate persona descriptions.

fits_no_version.finding: Student outputs remain PHLE-separable (AUC 0.92–0.94) even though behavioural transfer was absent or non-specific.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A decodable source signal can persist in distilled students without trait-specific behavioural transfer.

record.problems: The experiments use 7B models from two families, and hidden objectives are supplied in prompts rather than trained into models. The filtering judge is from the generator's model family. Each student uses a single training seed. The animal preference shift is not specific to owls, and the paper reports no numerical student harmfulness rate.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted the many PHLE header-mismatch, rewording, broader-header, and calibration table cells (Sections 4.6–4.7; Appendices D–F and J–K), as they concern detection-score sensitivity or calibration rather than the tested behavioral-transfer outcomes. The main detection results and the no-mention condition are retained above.

untested.parts: Animal preference transfer from text-trained students (only number students are reported); other traits; code or maths data; multiple seeds.
Not tested. Cross-family failure of transfer is only cited from Cloud et al.; the cross-family results are PHLE detection, not student transfer.
Only a prompted latent harm intent was tested, with no behaviourally misaligned teacher. No emergent-misalignment-style teacher was used.
Not tested; mechanism is discussed speculatively only (pre-training corpus elements, steering-vector citation).
Not tested; LoRA rank 16 only, no full fine-tuning, no prompt-variation analysis of transfer.

missing.what: Absolute owl-naming rate of owl number students: 0–2% of the time
Training details of the number students (10 epochs, batch size 16, LoRA r16, α=32) and the absence of any reported animal-preference result for text-trained animal students

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The student experiments are a small side check: one seed, LoRA only, 7B Olmo. The secret-harm teacher was itself not behaviourally harmful, which weakens R4 as a test of C. The reader's 'observed' states on R2/R3 mislabel comparator animals as trait effects.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests animal preference after training on filtered outputs, including number sequences, but does not establish broad transfer across other traits, datasets, or training methods.
No comparison of students initialized from the teacher's base model versus a different base model. Cross-family PHLE detection is not a test of cross-family student transfer.
The study checks harmful behavior on opportunity probes for secret-harm students; it does not test other alignment-relevant traits or a range of harmful behaviors.
No causal test identifying token entanglement, divergence tokens, a steering-vector-like direction, or a gradient mechanism.
The study uses LoRA rank 16 only; it does not compare full fine-tuning or other LoRA ranks. It does not systematically test robustness of behavioral transfer across evaluation prompts.
No prompt-only behavioral test without fine-tuning.

rows.subject: Olmo 3 Instruct student trained on owl-generator number sequences
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on filtered owl-generator number sequences; measured exact probability of naming animals as favorite.

conditions.value: 210 prompts: ten paraphrases, each asked plainly and after 20 random number lists
matched students trained on no-prompt generator answers

rows.measure: Relative probability of answering “owl” as favorite animal
rows.uncertainty: p ≤ 0.015, one-sided sign-flip test over the ten paraphrases
rows.note: The paper says it did not observe owl-specific behavioral transfer: other animal preferences rose by similar factors.
rows.check: Owl probability did rise 1.3–2.5× (p≤0.015), but absolute owl naming was only 0–2%. Dog (×1.33) and eagle (×3.05) rose similarly or more. The authors state they saw no owl-specific transfer. For a version about acquiring the specific trait, this is absent rather than partial.

source_check.problem: None. Appendix H never defines 'matched control students' for the animal students, so 'trained on no-prompt answers' is inferred. 'Absent' fits the authors' explicit 'no owl-specific transfer', though owl did rise significantly against control.

relation.reason: The distillation check reports its own owl-student transfer result, which bears on version A.

tranche.reason: Appendix H follows the Cloud et al. recipe: same-base prompted teacher (owl prompt wording), Cloud number prompt, students fine-tuned on outputs, favourite-animal question. Students are LoRA rank 16 with a single seed. The rest of the paper is PHLE detection and does not test transfer.

source_check.notes: Only Appendix H tests transfer, with one seed per student. It does not say whether the owl ×1.3–2.5 range covers number students only or also text students. Section 4.8 ties the 0–2% figure to number students. The student PHLE results (Figure 10) cover only secret-harm students. The paper is mainly a detection method (PHLE), and its cross-family results are about reading the signal, not about transfer (version B untested).

statements.correction: The owl ×1.3–2.5 rise (p ≤ 0.015) and the 0–2% absolute naming are the same exact-probability measurement over 210 prompts. Dog ×1.33 and eagle ×3.05 rose similarly or more. The authors: shift not specific to owls. This is a specificity issue (exact vs related trait), not relative vs absolute readout.
statements.problem: Presents the study as a readout disagreement (relative vs absolute). There is none: both numbers come from one measurement. The authors reject transfer because the rise is not owl-specific.

statements.correction: Teacher harmful on 5.8% of 120 opportunity-probe samples, same as no prompt. Students no more harmful than controls; no numeric student rate. Full transfer would also predict this null. Student outputs still PHLE-separable (0.92 ± 0.04 vs secret-friend, 0.94 ± 0.03 vs no-prompt students). Verdict should be none, not limits_scope.
statements.problem: The facts are right, but limits_scope does not follow. The teacher showed no harm on the same probes, so a student null is uninformative for C.

statements.correction: Secret-harm students no more harmful than controls on opportunity probes; teacher's own rate 5.8% = no-prompt rate. Student outputs PHLE-separable at AUC 0.92–0.94, so whether the intent transfers is not determined.
statements.problem: 'Does not transfer' overstates. The study shows no behavioural difference only, and the teacher showed none either. A latent signal does reach the students.

statements.correction: GPT-4.1 0.80 on owl vs trains numbers; prompted Olmo fully separates owl vs no-prompt text at higher k. PHLE 0.52 ± 0.07 on secret harm vs friend numbers; 0.56 ± 0.09 on no-mention owl vs eagle text. Cross-family shown for text (Figs 7, 9). Student AUC 0.92–0.94 is for secret-harm students only; no PHLE result for owl students.
statements.problem: Overgeneralises. Prompted classifiers are not always near chance. PHLE fails in some cells, cross-family is shown on text only, and the PHLE student results cover only secret-harm students.
